title: PA: Another District Clamping Down On Reading Rights
author: Peter Greene
summary: Peter Greene reports on the Penncrest School District in northwest Pennsylvania, where a board policy chair has repeatedly targeted library books that touch on LGBTQ lives or racism. He traces a pattern from a 2021 Facebook flap and a blocked teacher conference presentation to a July library policy and a December proposal banning anything sexualized or showing nudity. Greene's reading is that the vague standards are a vehicle for erasing LGBTQ persons from school libraries, with parents told to look elsewhere if they object. He notes the board member was re-elected and has supporters at meetings, and argues that this small rural fight is not merely local because the same story is playing out across the country.
points: A local board's library-policy revisions show how vague 'sexualized content' language can function as a ban on any depiction of LGBTQ people.
The restrictions are driven by one policy chair, but his re-election and supporters at meetings show he is not an isolated voice.
Telling parents to find objectionable material elsewhere shifts a small faction's preferences onto every family's children.
Greene frames a remote district's vote as part of a national pattern of limiting the right to read.
quotes: So just the facts, literary stuff is okay, maybe "art," and "ethical standards," though no guidance on whose ethics exactly.

Then there was the time they refused a teacher's request to go present at the state Pennsylvania Council of Teachers of English and Language Arts conference because some of the sessions at the conference sounded a little too critical race theory (her presentation was supposed to be about “Using Audio Analysis to Maximize Independent Reading Time”). Penncrest is once again focused on limiting the reading rights of its students.

So, no sexy stuff, no nudity. It doesn't have to rise to the level of porn, and Valesky has made it clear that any depiction at all of LGBTQ persons is over the line. And if parents object to the school district banning these works for everybody's kids, they can just go get the stuff on their own.
Valesky is the point man on all this LGBTQ panic, but it would be a mistake to imagine that he is a lone voice crying in the wilderness. He was successfully re-elected in 2019.

It's a small district far from big press and big city concerns. The selection of books for a school library is an issue that will always spark discussion and concern, but when a board considers erasing LGBTQ persons entirely or trying to convince young humans that sex is a big secret that they should never hear anything about or allowing the concerns of the most conservative members of a community to limit the right to read for all members--well, it's not just a local issue, and it is troubling. This story is being enacted all over the country; we'll see how this one plays out.
